newsitem.title: UK: Oil eases after hits five-year high on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Oil eases after hits five-year high on Iraq.

text.p: Oil prices hit a new post-Gulf War high on Thursday but later gave up most of the gains as a nervous market braced for another U.S. military strike against a defiant Iraq.
"The potential widening of the conflict (to areas that can produce oil) is a cause for concern," said Tom Holmes of brokers MeesPierson Derivatives.

World benchmark Brent crude oil futures traded as high as $24.39 a barrel, up 81 cents on the day and beating Wednesday's peak of $23.82 -- the highest prompt price on London's International Petroleum Exchange since the middle of the Gulf War in January 1991.

Profit-taking took Brent back to a low of $23.35 before Iraqi claims that its air defence units fired three missiles at U.S. and allied warplanes in southern Iraq ob Thursday sparked a modest rally. At 1610 GMT, October Brent stood at $23.69.
Oil prices now stand some $7 above this time last year and much higher than oil analysts had previously expected.

"It has gone beyond the loss of Iraqi oil. The market is worried about the crisis developing -- the fear of war," said Nigel Saperia, managing director of oil trading at Bankers Trust International in London.
Oil prices get a boost whenever vital fuel supplies are threatened in the Gulf area which contains nearly 70 percent of the world's oil reserves and produces about a quarter of global oil supplies.
With nearly every other oil producer running at full throttle, only Saudi Arabia and ironically Iraq have the ability to meet any serious supply shortfall.
Saudi Arabia is the world's largest oil producer and exporter and its 8.0 million barrel per day output makes use of about 80 percent of its capacity.

Iraq could probably produce about two million bpd if a United Nations embargo was lifted but the chances of that are growing slimmer by the day. A U.N plan to allow limited Iraqi exports appears on ice for now, analysts said.

"At some stage the market will take stock and accept that there is a supply disruption. The reality is that the Iraqi oil sale is choked for an indefinite period of time," said Peter Gignoux, head of the London energy desk at Smith, Barney.

Earlier this year, oil market pundits warned of a price crash if members of the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) like Saudi Arabia did not make way for the return of Iraqi exports which had been expected as early as this month under a U.N. deal.

It would have allowed Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to raise funds for humanitarian supplies, but it was suspended after Iraqi troops moved into Kurdish areas last week, drawing U.S. retaliatory strikes.

Robust demand and shortfalls in non-OPEC production because of bad weather and technical mishaps has meant that the market now will miss the estimated 700,000 barrels per day of Iraqi oil it once feared.
"The truth is we now need that Iraqi oil," said Leo Drollas, chief economist at the Centre for Global Energy Studies.
Though panic buying took Brent to a record $40.95 in October 1990 when Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait, traders say the current buying spree is backed up by bullish fundamentals.
Oil analysts and traders say low oil inventories in the U.S. and Europe, especially of heating fuel, and robust demand would have resulted in firm oil prices even without the current Iraqi tensions.
